[[:db/retract 17592186129481 :question/answer-fields 17592186126386] [:db/retract 17592186198778 :question/answer-fields 17592186195379] [:db/retract 17592186069334 :question/answer-fields 17592186067174] [:db/retract 17592186064888 :question/answer-fields 17592186063384] {:db/id 17592186129481 :question/worked-solution "Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting 

$$
a=3i+2j,\,u=-7i-6j,\,v=2i
$$

into the equation above, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\ 2i & =(-7i-6j)+(3i+2j)t \\ 9i+6j & =(3i+2j)t \\ 9i+6j & =3ti+2tj\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the $i$ and $j$ components in the last equation, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}9=3t \\ 6=2t\end{aligned}\,⟹\,t=3\,\text{s}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198778 :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times N
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in N\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f8/f8808e4c35775c754dab0bf328a8d129e423009e18ec5f4b962461eba2afcea2.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $2.$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,2)\,:\,x\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/a5/a51fe9dc5bf7c55b01f72a45d4b88bde4653f0d3da85c1231b0d54c76a6e8c81.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

![](images/7a/7ae3c488e60d3dcda304649e575a7d2efc54be7262a54d0455550af420c39b68.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069334 :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-2x+3 &  \\ y=\frac{2}{x-2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get a quadratic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3 & =\frac{2}{x-2}+1 \\ -2x+2 & =\frac{2}{x-2} \\ (-2x+2)(x-2) & =2 \\ 2(-x+1)(x-2) & =2 \\ (-x+1)(x-2) & =1 \\ -{x}^{2}+3x-2 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the quadratic formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{{3}^{2}-4(1)(3)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{9-12}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{-3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The square root of a negative number is not a real number, so there are no real solutions. Consequently, the line $y=-2x+3$ does not intersect the hyperbola $y=\frac{2}{x-2}+1.$

A sketch of the situation is shown below.

![](images/41/41fee04552a47d93f1dbd788e69e12c4b58e377ec4c0b63c3ed55c712d337f94.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064888 :question/problem "For what reason does the function $f(x)$ below have a discontinuity at $x=-1?$ 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+x, & x<-1 \\ {x}^{2}+1, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]}]

have a discontinuity at $x=-1?$ 

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+x, & x<-1 \\ {x}^{2}+1, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(-1)=(-1)^{2}+1=2,$ so $f(-1)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}({x}^{3}+x) \\  & =(-1)^{3}+(-1) \\  & =-2, \\ {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\,\,\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1$ because ${lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x).$"} {:db/id 17592186233080 :question/id #uuid $(p,q),$ then $p+q=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-2x+3 &  \\ y=\frac{2}{x-2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get a quadratic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3 & =\frac{2}{x-2}+1 \\ -2x+2 & =\frac{2}{x-2} \\ (-2x+2)(x-2) & =2 \\ 2(-x+1)(x-2) & =2 \\ (-x+1)(x-2) & =1 \\ -{x}^{2}+3x-2 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the quadratic formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{{3}^{2}-4(1)(3)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{9-12}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{-3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The square root of a negative number is not a real number, so there are no real solutions. Consequently, the line $y=-2x+3$ does not intersect the hyperbola $y=\frac{2}{x-2}+1.$

$(-7i-6j)\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}.$ Find the time when the velocity of the particle equals $2i\,\text{m/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting 

$$
a=3i+2j,\,u=-7i-6j,\,v=2i
$$

into the equation above, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\ 2i & =(-7i-6j)+(3i+2j)t \\ 9i+6j & =(3i+2j)t \\ 9i+6j & =3ti+2tj\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the $i$ and $j$ components in the last equation, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}9=3t \\ 6=2t\end{aligned}\,⟹\,t=3\,\text{s}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129482 :question/id #uuid "cf5bf00a-e492-5d4d-9f8a-0af5a0102f4d" :question/math-academy-id "q-136293"} {:db/id 17592186269115 :question/id #uuid Cartesian plane?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times N
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in N}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}={(x,1)\,:\,x\in R}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f8/f8808e4c35775c754dab0bf328a8d129e423009e18ec5f4b962461eba2afcea2.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $2.$

$$
{S}_{2}={(x,2)\,:\,x\in R}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/a5/a51fe9dc5bf7c55b01f72a45d4b88bde4653f0d3da85c1231b0d54c76a6e8c81.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199560 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $A$ and $B$ are sets, the Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](images/07/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space. 

![](images/e7/e74fb5948144bc61173e4de73865cb746278bd31fd87e4abf927fa01821ba936.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "c18e6618-573b-5560-8d95-58ed56f05155" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c7652427-e5ff-5d02-9f23-39039f090aff" :step/math-academy-id 153383 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199078}} {:db/id 17592186199078 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198272 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198169 :question/id #uuid "bb40c174-3739-50df-835e-5d47c9902d5b" :question/math-academy-id "e-13192"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c3a2b291-c6dd-58c8-a10f-d851511d7bfc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048899} {:db/id 17592186050367} {:db/id 17592186050432} {:db/id 17592186050763} {:db/id 17592186050923}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198802} {:db/id 17592186198807} {:db/id 17592186287775} {:db/id 17592186287870} {:db/id 17592186287871} {:db/id 17592186389895} {:db/id 17592186390326} {:db/id 17592186421830}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane"} :step/id #uuid "2190f1df-5853-5d8c-85e2-33f40f1f0f24" :step/math-academy-id 153384 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199079}} {:db/id 17592186199079 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199579 :tutorial/content "Cartesian coordinates can also be used to visualize other Cartesian products.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](images/ca/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

![](images/03/033c40b86bfd5cebf24d34de644f632213207386c2b67c559af7594468599e1e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "1626e562-8e88-5ff3-bae3-4162438c0086" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8329 :tutorial/title "Cartesian Products of Countably Infinite Sets"} :step/id #uuid "cd371945-c79b-5b78-9017-15c39e4d5ed7" :step/math-academy-id 153387 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199080}} {:db/id 17592186199080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198273 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198154 :question/id #uuid "eae94514-cd92-5405-90b1-ee09dad18e13" :question/math-academy-id "e-13162"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2aee319-68d6-54f7-8023-b24d32610bc4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050088}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198778} {:db/id 17592186198779} {:db/id 17592186287749} {:db/id 17592186287752} {:db/id 17592186287753} {:db/id 17592186287777} {:db/id 17592186287784} {:db/id 17592186287787} {:db/id 17592186389909} {:db/id 17592186389916}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane"} :step/id #uuid "48b1fb46-7071-5897-9dd7-a47e1d955f6c" :step/math-academy-id 153388 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199081}} {:db/id 17592186199081 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199584 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch a representation of the set $S= [0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the Cartesian plane.

The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S = [0,1] \times [0, 1]
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=
\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in [0,1],\, y\in [0,1] \big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_0 \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}0}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{red}0} = \big\{ ({\color{red}{0}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

We can represent $S_{\color{red}0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general $S_{\color{blue}{i}} \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{blue}{i}} = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{i}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

For each ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1],$ $S_{\color{blue}{i}}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $({\color{blue}{i}},0)$ to the point $({\color{blue}{i}},1).$

![](images/28/28b9aa0559635ed4090f10dd0b59f2cbb6c297f8736d9509a637b5d78d27561c.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I = [0,1]{:}$

$$
S = \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}.
$$

As $\color{blue}i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}{:}$

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](images/ca/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S = [0,1] \times [0, 1]
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=
\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in [0,1],\, y\in [0,1] \big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_0 \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}0}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{red}0} = \big\{ ({\color{red}{0}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

We can represent $S_{\color{red}0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general $S_{\color{blue}{i}} \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{blue}{i}} = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{i}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

For each ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1],$ $S_{\color{blue}{i}}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $({\color{blue}{i}},0)$ to the point $({\color{blue}{i}},1).$

![](images/28/28b9aa0559635ed4090f10dd0b59f2cbb6c297f8736d9509a637b5d78d27561c.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I = [0,1]{:}$

$$
S = \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}.
$$

As $\color{blue}i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}{:}$

:tutorial/content "When considering the intersection of a line and a reciprocal function, three possibilities can occur.

The first possibility is that there are two intersection points, as illustrated in the example below.

![](images/00/00f19933ef5f2e7879012dbd9b87fd86964ed44b74e54749dccd2186e02e2a6a.png)

The second possibility is that there is only one intersection point. For example:

![](images/aa/aabf0d5ea18c01842890b6e470d7c8eaaf36371565ff7c271ea2ab24ccfc9565.png)

The final possibility is that there are no intersection points. For example:

![](images/da/da7ecba1887505f162144ab3b86e4cca9be104cda7e78ba8fef3d02f10de2abc.png)

Typically, when computing the points of intersection of a reciprocal function and a line, we have to solve a system of two equations. In the first graph that was shown above, this system was

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=x \\ y=\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This system of equations can (usually) be transformed into a single rational equation, which can itself be converted into a quadratic equation. For the above system, we have

$$
x = \dfrac{1}{x} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x^2 = 1.
$$

By solving the quadratic equation, we can find the intersection points. And like quadratic equations, there can be two, one, or no real solutions. In this case, there are two solutions:

$$
x^2 = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = \pm 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "70a19ea7-8a66-5b98-b7a2-2312cfe9cf44" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3403 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b6e2fa7-06cd-5725-9235-7ae5c5dbd6a0" :step/math-academy-id 466045 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069851}} {:db/id 17592186069851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068884 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068602 :question/id #uuid "ffb2b712-52b9-5a09-9ac4-10a88f72f57e" :question/math-academy-id "e-5193"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4fafc8c8-0452-582f-b603-6f633de9a39a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048891} {:db/id 17592186049832} {:db/id 17592186049869}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069272} {:db/id 17592186069335} {:db/id 17592186069345} {:db/id 17592186259595} {:db/id 17592186292930} {:db/id 17592186292931} {:db/id 17592186292932}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Intersection Points in the Case of Two Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "674f9cf9-a5de-5045-b6cb-e0e31e295966" :step/math-academy-id 466046 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069852}} {:db/id 17592186069852 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069983 :tutorial/content "Let's now turn our attention to the cases where a line and a reciprocal function intersect at either one point or no points.

For example, suppose that we want to find where the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x}+1$ and the line $y=2$ intersect. To do this, we need to solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{1}{x}+1 \\ y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal and solving for $x,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+1 & =2 \\ \frac{1}{x} & =1 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the corresponding $y$-coordinate, we plug $x=1$ into either equation. Let's choose the first equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{x}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{1}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $\left(1,\,2 \right)$.

A sketch of the situation is shown below.

For example, suppose that we want to find where the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x}+1$ and the line $y=2$ intersect. To do this, we need to solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{1}{x}+1 \\ y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal and solving for $x,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+1 & =2 \\ \frac{1}{x} & =1 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the corresponding $y$-coordinate, we plug $x=1$ into either equation. Let's choose the first equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{x}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{1}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $\left(1,\,2 \right)$.

A sketch of the situation is shown below.

"Intuitively, a function $f(x)$ is **continuous** if we can draw $y=f(x)$ without taking our pen off the paper. 

We can give a precise mathematical definition of continuity using limits:

> *A function $f(x)$ is **continuous at the point** $\boldsymbol{x=c}$ if*
> 
> 
> $$
> \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c).
> $$

In other words, a function is continuous at a point if the limit at the point is equal to the function value at the point.

To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

- Does $f(c)$ exist? In other words, we must check that $f(x)$ is defined at $x=c.$

- Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist? In other words, we have to check that $\displaystyle \lim_{x \to c^{-}}f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^{+}}f(x).$

- Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)?$

If the answer to all three questions is yes, then the function is continuous at $x=c.$ If the function is not continuous at $x=c,$ we say that it has a **discontinuity** at $x=c.$

The diagram below shows a function that's continuous at $x=c.$

![](images/54/54ebdb8faa4b1ece5620b817b813780e8abd5cc89cf858eed4cb9ba03f24a046.png)

Notice that:

- $f(c)$ exists$\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $\lim\limits_{x\to c}f(x)$ exists $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $\lim\limits_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)$ $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

Let's now see how to use these continuity conditions to check for continuity in a piecewise function." :tutorial/id #uuid "4a7b79ea-d89f-5d21-948b-8a735e641995" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6695 We can use vectors to model the acceleration of a particle moving in the $xy$-plane. 

For example, consider a particle $P$ whose acceleration vector $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\mathbf a = (3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\,\textrm{m/s}^2.
$$

We should think of this particle's acceleration as being made up of two components: 

- a *horizontal* component of $3 \: \textrm{m/s}^2$ (to the right), and

- a *vertical* component of $4 \: \textrm{m/s}^2$ (upward).

In other words,

- the horizontal component of the velocity increases by $3\,\textrm{m/s}$ every second, and

- the vertical component of the velocity increases by $4\,\textrm{m/s}$ every second.

Also, since both components are constants, we say that this particle moves with **constant acceleration**.

If a particle is moving with constant acceleration, the velocity vector $\mathbf v$ at time $t$ can be found using

$$
\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,
$$

where $\mathbf{u}$ is the velocity of the particle when $t=0$ (i.e., the **initial velocity**).

For example, suppose that the initial velocity of our particle is given by $\mathbf{u} = (2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}.$ What is the particle's velocity when $t=2 \, \textrm{s}?$

Substituting our data into the formula above, we obtain that the velocity of the particle will be

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\  & =(2i+3j)+(3i+4j)(2) \\  & =(2i+3j)+(6i+8j) \\  & =(8i+11j)\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e71afcde-f4ec-52b0-bc4b-041b528e32f6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6063 :tutorial/title "Relating Velocity and Acceleration"} :step/id #uuid "2d22baec-c09f-5f9f-b2ee-f15b2c144f57" 1074 "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times N
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in N}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}={(x,1)\,:\,x\in R}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f8/f8808e4c35775c754dab0bf328a8d129e423009e18ec5f4b962461eba2afcea2.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $2.$

$$
{S}_{2}={(x,2)\,:\,x\in R}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/a5/a51fe9dc5bf7c55b01f72a45d4b88bde4653f0d3da85c1231b0d54c76a6e8c81.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$

$$

$$

$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](images/07/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space. 

![](images/e7/e74fb5948144bc61173e4de73865cb746278bd31fd87e4abf927fa01821ba936.png)" 17592186045417] [17592186199560 1065 8237 17592186045417] [17592186199560 1066 #uuid "c18e6618-573b-5560-8d95-58ed56f05155" 17592186045417] [17592186199560 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186199579 1064 "Cartesian coordinates can also be used to visualize other Cartesian products.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](images/ca/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S = [0,1] \times [0, 1]
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=
\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in [0,1],\, y\in [0,1] \big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_0 \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}0}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{red}0} = \big\{ ({\color{red}{0}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

We can represent $S_{\color{red}0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general $S_{\color{blue}{i}} \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{blue}{i}} = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{i}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

For each ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1],$ $S_{\color{blue}{i}}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $({\color{blue}{i}},0)$ to the point $({\color{blue}{i}},1).$

![](images/28/28b9aa0559635ed4090f10dd0b59f2cbb6c297f8736d9509a637b5d78d27561c.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I = [0,1]{:}$

$$
S = \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}.
$$

As $\color{blue}i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}{:}$
